title: AI Tutoring with Khanmigo in a Two-Year School Experiment
content:
Student Opinion Scale
Category: Student Learning
Generative AI has been promoted as the technology that could transform education by providing every student a personal tutor. We provide some of the first large-scale experimental evidence, from a two-year cluster randomized trial in 18 Tennessee middle schools in which randomly assigned students used Khan Academy with its AI tutor, Khanmigo, configured to coach rather than give answers, during existing daily remedial mathematics sessions. Assignment raises math achievement by 1.3 national percentile ranks per term, or about 0.06 to 0.08 standard deviations over a school year; the implied effect of a full year of active participation reaches 0.14 standard deviations. These gains resemble those from Khan Academy practice without AI assistance. One explanation is that students used the tutor infrequently and, when they did, rarely engaged it in substantive mathematical dialogue: 96 percent of students tried Khanmigo at least once, but the median student messaged it on only a third of the days they practiced, and in only 17 percent of the exercise sessions in which they made a mistake. Messages that students did send were mostly bare answers or clicks on suggested prompts. The binding constraint appears to be engagement: realizing the promise of AI tutoring will require getting students to use it, not just giving them access.

report.summary: Two-year randomized trial finds Khanmigo AI tutoring in Tennessee middle schools raised math achievement modestly, with low student engagement limiting impact.
report.background: Generative AI has been promoted as a way to give every student a personal tutor, but rigorous evidence on whether AI tutors actually improve learning remains limited. Khan Academy's Khanmigo is one of the most widely deployed AI tutoring tools, built on large language models and designed to coach students rather than provide answers. This study offers some of the first large-scale experimental evidence: a two-year cluster randomized trial across 18 Tennessee middle schools. Randomly assigned students used Khan Academy with Khanmigo during existing daily remedial mathematics sessions. The trial tested whether AI tutoring can boost math achievement under real-world conditions, where student motivation, teacher support, and implementation quality vary widely.
key_points: The randomized trial found modest achievement gains: about 1.3 national percentile ranks per term, or 0.06 to 0.08 standard deviations over a school year. A full year of active participation implied roughly 0.14 standard deviations. These effects resemble gains from using Khan Academy practice without AI assistance, suggesting Khanmigo added little measurable benefit in this setting.

Student engagement was strikingly low. Although 96 percent of students tried Khanmigo at least once, the median student messaged it on only a third of the days they practiced math. In sessions where students made a mistake, only 17 percent used the tutor at all. Most messages were bare answers or clicks on suggested prompts.

Khanmigo was configured to coach rather than give answers, a design meant to encourage reasoning. But the constraint appears to be getting students to use the tutor, not merely giving them access. Access alone did not translate into substantive mathematical dialogue or sustained help-seeking.

The results challenge the idea that AI tutoring automatically transforms learning. Gains were similar to Khan Academy without AI, implying that the AI layer may not have changed outcomes much. Implementation, student habits, and integration into instruction likely matter more than the technology itself.

For schools and edtech developers, the study highlights a need to design for engagement: onboarding, teacher training, prompts that spark dialogue, and accountability may be essential. Measuring usage and learning outcomes together will be critical before scaling AI tutors.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this trial is a reality check: adding a large language model to an established learning platform does not guarantee better learning. Developers should focus on engagement mechanics, dialogue quality, and measurable outcomes rather than access alone. For educators and parents, it suggests AI tutors are not a substitute for motivated practice or teacher support. For regular users, AI tutoring can still help, but benefits depend on active, sustained use. The broader lesson is that implementation and human behavior often constrain AI's impact more than model capability, shaping how schools, investors, and policymakers evaluate generative AI in education.
report.tools: Watch Khanmigo and Khan Academy for updates, plus Stanford's Tutor CoPilot, Google's LearnLM/Gemini for Education, and Carnegie Learning's MATHia. Open-source options include Llama-based tutoring stacks, Open TutorAI, and learning-analytics dashboards. Researchers can examine Khan Academy's public reports, EdWorkingPapers, and initiatives like the Learning Engineering Virtual Institute for replication data and implementation insights.
